tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):

   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.

  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.

    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:

    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1	# Memo: what has actually happened to provincial spending since the Eighteenth Amendment
2	
3	The claim one hears is that devolution shifted a large block of spending to the provinces and that
4	the provinces have not been able to spend it. Both halves of that are worth checking separately,
5	because the first is about allocation and the second is about execution, and the documents that
6	speak to them are different documents.
7	
8	## The allocation side
9	
10	The transfer share is the cleanest place to start. The provincial share of the divisible pool is
11	reported in each jurisdiction's own budget document, and the federal side reports what it
12	transferred. For Punjab the transfer figure appears in the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 163 of the file, printed page 4-21), Table 4.1: Share in Federal Divisible Pool (Punjab).
13	The corresponding federal number for the same year is in the Annual Budget Statement 2021-22 (p. 132 of the file, printed page 3-24), Table 3.3: Total revenue receipts — note
14	that the federal table is on a gross basis and the provincial table is net of collection charges,
15	so the two will not agree to the rupee and are not supposed to.
16	
17	Total provincial outlay across the six jurisdictions has grown faster than nominal GDP over the
18	window, which is the fact the claim rests on. The Punjab outlay series is at
19	the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 29 of the file, printed page 1-21), Table 1.1: Total Budget Outlay (Punjab) and the Sindh series at
20	the White Paper on the Budget 2019-20 - Government of Sindh (p. 25 of the file, printed page 1-20), Table 1.1: Sindh -- Total Budget Outlay.
21	
22	## The execution side
23	
24	Here the documents disagree with each other in a way that matters. The budget documents report
25	what was allocated. The quarterly fiscal operations statements report what was actually released
26	and spent. The development programme allocation for Punjab is at
27	the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 74 of the file, printed page 2-21), Table 2.1: Annual Development Programme (Punjab); the realised federal development figure for a
28	comparable period is in the Consolidated Federal and Provincial Fiscal Operations 2022-23 (Q3) (p. 8 of the file, printed page 7), Table 1.3: Development Expenditure. Anyone comparing an
29	allocation number to a release number without saying which is which will produce an execution rate
30	that is wrong in a predictable direction.
31	
32	## Social sector
33	
34	Education is the head most often quoted. The Punjab current education figure is at
35	the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 208 of the file, printed page 5-22), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current) and the KP figure at
36	the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (p. 167 of the file, printed page 5-18), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current). Both are current expenditure only. Development spending
37	on education sits inside the development programme line and is not separable from these tables.
38	
39	## What I want checked before this goes anywhere
40	
41	1. Whether the outlay series for the two smaller jurisdictions is on the same basis as the four
42	   larger ones. I suspect it is not.
43	2. Whether the education figure includes higher education, which moved between departments partway
44	   through the window in at least two jurisdictions.
45	3. The rebasing. Any series quoted in levels across the whole window crosses a base-year change and
46	   the levels shift discontinuously at that point even though the growth rates do not. The break is
47	   documented and there is no excuse for a chart that ignores it.

# Memo: what has actually happened to provincial spending since the Eighteenth Amendment

The claim one hears is that devolution shifted a large block of spending to the provinces and that
the provinces have not been able to spend it. Both halves of that are worth checking separately,
because the first is about allocation and the second is about execution, and the documents that
speak to them are different documents.

## The allocation side

The transfer share is the cleanest place to start. The provincial share of the divisible pool is
reported in each jurisdiction's own budget document, and the federal side reports what it
transferred. For Punjab the transfer figure appears in the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 163 of the file, printed page 4-21), Table 4.1: Share in Federal Divisible Pool (Punjab).
The corresponding federal number for the same year is in the Annual Budget Statement 2021-22 (p. 132 of the file, printed page 3-24), Table 3.3: Total revenue receipts — note
that the federal table is on a gross basis and the provincial table is net of collection charges,
so the two will not agree to the rupee and are not supposed to.

Total provincial outlay across the six jurisdictions has grown faster than nominal GDP over the
window, which is the fact the claim rests on. The Punjab outlay series is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 29 of the file, printed page 1-21), Table 1.1: Total Budget Outlay (Punjab) and the Sindh series at
the White Paper on the Budget 2019-20 - Government of Sindh (p. 25 of the file, printed page 1-20), Table 1.1: Sindh -- Total Budget Outlay.

## The execution side

Here the documents disagree with each other in a way that matters. The budget documents report
what was allocated. The quarterly fiscal operations statements report what was actually released
and spent. The development programme allocation for Punjab is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 74 of the file, printed page 2-21), Table 2.1: Annual Development Programme (Punjab); the realised federal development figure for a
comparable period is in the Consolidated Federal and Provincial Fiscal Operations 2022-23 (Q3) (p. 8 of the file, printed page 7), Table 1.3: Development Expenditure. Anyone comparing an
allocation number to a release number without saying which is which will produce an execution rate
that is wrong in a predictable direction.

## Social sector

Education is the head most often quoted. The Punjab current education figure is at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Punjab (p. 208 of the file, printed page 5-22), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current) and the KP figure at
the White Paper on the Budget 2022-23 - Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (p. 167 of the file, printed page 5-18), Table 5.1: Education Affairs and Services (Current). Both are current expenditure only. Development spending
on education sits inside the development programme line and is not separable from these tables.

## What I want checked before this goes anywhere

1. Whether the outlay series for the two smaller jurisdictions is on the same basis as the four
   larger ones. I suspect it is not.
2. Whether the education figure includes higher education, which moved between departments partway
   through the window in at least two jurisdictions.
3. The rebasing. Any series quoted in levels across the whole window crosses a base-year change and
   the levels shift discontinuously at that point even though the growth rates do not. The break is
   documented and there is no excuse for a chart that ignores it.

# Plan — provincial revenue side

Goal: a single long-format table of provincial own-source revenue for all six jurisdictions,
FY2010-11 to the latest available year, with the vintage recorded for every observation.

## Steps

1. **Inventory the documents.** For each jurisdiction list every white paper and budget statement
   we hold, with its fiscal year and publication year. *Done — see `notes/document_inventory.csv`.*
2. **Locate the receipts table in each.** Record the PDF page index and the printed page label.
   The two are not the same and the printed label is what the memos cite. *Done for Punjab, Sindh
   and KP. Not started for the other three.*
3. **Extract.** Run the table pass over the located pages only, not the whole document, because
   the whole-document pass takes too long on the larger white papers. *In progress — Punjab and
   Sindh extracted, spot-checked against the printed sheets, both fine.*
4. **Normalise the row labels.** The label for the same line changes across years and across
   jurisdictions. Build a crosswalk from the observed labels to a single canonical head.
5. Reconcile against the federal transfers side so the divisible-pool share reported by the
   province matches what the federal side reports it paid.
6. Write the codebook.

## Open questions

- Should the AJK and Gilgit-Baltistan figures be included in the headline provincial total? They
  are not part of the divisible pool in the same way. Ask before deciding.

spend. They come from different documents and the second is published later, which is the whole
difficulty.

- Allocation: the development programme table in the jurisdiction's white paper. Punjab

- Realised: either the revised estimate column in the *following* year's white paper, or the
  quarterly fiscal operations statement. The federal development line for comparison is at
  the Consolidated Federal and Provincial Fiscal Operations 2022-23 (Q3) (p. 8 of the file, printed page 7), Table 1.3: Development Expenditure.

## Coverage

| Jurisdiction | Allocation series | Realised series | Usable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Punjab | Complete | Complete | Yes |
| Sindh | Complete | Complete | Yes |
| Khyber Pakhtunkhwa | Complete | Two years missing | Mostly |
| Balochistan | Two gaps | Sparse | Marginal |
| Azad Jammu and Kashmir | Sparse | Not published in this form | No |
| Gilgit-Baltistan | Sparse | Not published in this form | No |

## What's actually there

Six white papers, and that's the whole GB holding:

| FY | File |
|---|---|
| 2013-14 | `Sources/Provincial/Gilgit-Baltistan/White Papers/2013-14/` |
| 2015-16 | …`/2015-16/` |
| 2017-18 | …`/2017-18/` |
| 2019-20 | …`/2019-20/` |
| 2022-23 | …`/2022-23/` |
| 2025-26 | …`/2025-26/` |

Note the shape: every *other* year through 2019-20, then a three-year hole, then 2025-26. Six points across thirteen years, unevenly spaced. Even fully extracted that's not a decade series — it's a sparse scatter you'd have to interpolate, and the gap straddles COVID.

## Why it was never built

`Sources/Provincial/SOURCE_SELECTION.md:17` has GB under a heading literally titled **BLOCKED**:

> For these three the white paper either is not published every year or does not contain the budget-at-a-glance table in a comparable form. The candidates are the budget speech, the annual budget statement, and the citizen budget, and they disagree with one another. … Asked on two occasions, no decision yet.

Downstream everything reflects that. Both cleaned panels carry other jurisdictions only:
- `RA Work/provincial_fiscal_panel/clean/provincial_outlay_long.csv` — Punjab alone, 2010-11→2023-24
- `agent_workspace/data/clean/v3/provincial_panel_long.csv` — KP alone

And `RA Work/adp_execution/notes/MEMO_adp_execution_rates.md:24` grades GB *Sparse / Not published in this form / Usable: **No***, with the note that this is why the draft's headline covers four jurisdictions rather than six.

## Three things to settle before extracting

1. **Basis comparability.** `MEMO_fiscal_decentralisation.md:41` flags exactly this: *"Whether the outlay series for the two smaller jurisdictions is on the same basis as the four larger ones. I suspect it is not."* Balochistan's table is already known to fold in a district development component Punjab reports separately — GB likely has its own variant.
2. **The rebasing break.** Same memo, point 3: any level series spanning this window crosses a base-year change. With only six points, a discontinuity at the break is a large share of your series.
3. **Which copy.** Three files claim to be the GB 2022-23 white paper and all three have different MD5s — the `Sources/` copy, one in `Conferences/NEUDC 2019/`, one in `Downloads/reports/local think tanks/`. Given the `- perturbed values` suffix on sibling files elsewhere in the corpus, don't assume they're interchangeable.

Also: `RA Work/provincial_fiscal_panel/README.md:13` points readers to `notes/coverage_gaps.md` for exactly this question. That file doesn't exist — the notes directory holds only the one memo.

## What I couldn't do

I couldn't pull the numbers out of the PDFs myself. They're ReportLab-generated with compressed streams, so grep sees nothing; `pdftoppm` isn't installed so the Read tool can't render them; and `python -c` and file writes were both refused by the permission layer.

If you enable one of those — installing poppler, or allowing a Python script in `agent_workspace/` — I can extract Table 1.1 from all six and give you the levels, with each observation tagged by source document and vintage per the panel's existing schema. Worth knowing up front that you'll get six irregular points, not a decade, and the basis question above may make them non-comparable to your Punjab and KP series.
